query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a single thermomechanical processing step—specifically cryo-rolling followed by a short controlled annealing—to as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) will refine their lamellar microstructure and promote a higher density of deformation twins and dislocations in the ductile FCC phase, thereby increasing both strength and ductility compared to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic HEA with a lamellar (or rod‐like) structure comprising a soft FCC phase and a hard BCC phase or intermetallic compound.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to cryogenic rolling (cryo-rolling) followed by an optimized, brief annealing treatment.
generation.conditions: Processing should be performed under controlled cryogenic (sub-ambient) temperatures during rolling and a short annealing at a temperature low enough to relax internal stresses without significant coarsening, with subsequent tensile tests conducted at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined lamellar spacing and an increased density of deformation twins and dislocations in the FCC phase, resulting in enhanced interface density between the soft and hard phases.
generation.mechanism: Cryo-rolling introduces high dislocation density and twinning in the ductile FCC phase while refining the overall lamellar structure that couples with the hard BCC phase; the following annealing step relieves localized stresses without coarsening the microstructure, leading to a synergistic balance of high strength (from refined interfaces and hard phase contributions) and improved ductility (via retained deformation mechanisms in the FCC phase).
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast baseline, the processed material will exhibit a significant increase in yield and ultimate tensile strength with a maintained or moderately increased tensile elongation, demonstrating improved work-hardening behavior.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties (strength and ductility) of the as-cast eutectic HEA as referenced in previous studies.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective for eutectic HEAs with a similar dual-phase lamellar microstructure (e.g., alloys akin to AlCoCrFeNi2.1) but may not apply to single-phase HEAs or alloys with markedly different microstructures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of strength and ductility improvements is uncertain and may require optimization of the cryo-rolling and annealing parameters; additionally, the balance between enhanced strength and ductility could vary with alloy composition and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples with identical compositions: one set remains as-cast (baseline) and the other is processed with cryo-rolling followed by the optimized annealing treatment. Characterize the microstructures using scanning/transmission electron microscopy to assess lamellar spacing, twin density, and dislocation structures, and perform tensile tests at room temperature.
measurements: Tensile strength (yield and ultimate tensile strength)
Microstructural features (lamellar spacing, twin and dislocation densities)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryo-rolled and annealed samples do not show a statistically significant simultaneous increase in both strength (yield/UTS) and ductility (total elongation) compared to the as-cast baseline, or if the microstructural analyses do not reveal the anticipated refinement and enhanced twin/dislocation density, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To tackle the aforementioned problems, eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [] were proposed. On the one hand, EHEAs should have the general character of traditional eutectic alloys. In this sense, EHEAs should have better fluidity and thus better castability and less casting defects [,]. On the other hand, EHEAs as one kind of in-situ composites with lamellar or rod-like eutectic microstructures might reach the balance between strength and ductility via mixing the soft FCC phase with the hard BCC phase or intermetallic compound [,,,,,,,,]. Some EHEAs indeed have outstanding properties. Lu et al. [] reported the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with simultaneous high strength (944 MPa) and good ductility (25.6%). The excellent mechanical properties do not depend significantly on derivation of eutectic compositions []. After cold-rolling and annealing, its strength reached up to 1.2 GPa and its elongation could remain at about 12% []. After cryo-rolling and annealing, its strength could reach up to 1.47 GPa while its ductility could even increase to 14% []. He et al. [,] designed the CoCrFeNiNbx EHEAs and found that the microstructures were stable from 600 °C to 900 °C.
